URL test: the new dimensions round-trip through `?filters=`. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Flow metrics — a board view derived from movement history
tasks.description: P2, and the biggest item here: a read-only analytics view per board — cycle time, lead time, throughput and a cumulative flow diagram — built from recorded lane transitions. All three competitors have this and Flowline has none of it.
tasks.details: The enabler first: `ItemLogKind` gains a `moved` event carrying the destination lane id, written on every card transition (`moveCard`, `moveCardsToLane`, and the paths that relocate a card as a side effect). Then derive, never store: lead time (created to resolved), cycle time (first committed to resolved), throughput per period, and a cumulative flow diagram of items per stage over time. Record the *stage* the card moved into, not the lane id alone, so a team renaming or splitting its columns cannot corrupt its own history — the two-workflow rule paying off again, since the cards workflow is free to change shape while the four stages stay fixed. A new view alongside Dashboard and Objectives, addressable as `?board=<id>&view=metrics`, read-only and derived: no manual reporting, no targets to maintain, no AI summary. Scope the first slice to the cards workflow; the initiatives view can come later from the same history. History starts the day this ships, so back-date a set of transitions in the demo seed, otherwise the view is empty and proves nothing. Monte Carlo forecasting is explicitly out of scope. Persist bump: additive log kind, no backfill.
tasks.testStrategy: Pure derivation tests over synthetic histories: lead and cycle time including the never-resolved and moved-back cases, throughput buckets, and a CFD series where one card skipped a stage, one moved backwards and one was archived mid-flight. Store test that every move path writes exactly one `moved` event and that a same-lane move writes none. Regression test that renaming or splitting a lane after the fact leaves historical stage untouched. Migration test for the new log kind. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Item panel: redesign the drawer — header, tabs, property grid, comment footer
tasks.description: P1 UI: redesign the right-hand drawer into a compact, tabbed panel — a title block, a Details / Hierarchy & Links / Activity tab strip, a two-column property grid, a strategic-impact card and a sticky comment composer. It stays a drawer: a centred modal was considered and rejected because it covers the board you are working against.
tasks.details: Keep the drawer. `ItemPanel` stays the 400px `<aside data-item-panel>` flex sibling of the board in App.tsx — a centred modal was considered and rejected because it covers the board you are working against. What changes is everything inside it: thirteen stacked sections in one long scroll become a compact header plus three tabs. HEADER. A breadcrumb line — the lineage path from the top, ending in the current ref — with the panel actions on the right (add link, focus/lens, the card menu, close). Below it a title block: the ref chip and a context chip on the left, the block action on the right, and the title as a large editable heading. Nothing else competes with the title. TABS. Details / Hierarchy & Links / Activity, each carrying a count where it has one. The tabs are the real fix for the panel as it stands: what you look at while working (properties, spec, sub-tasks, acceptance criteria) is separate from what you consult (lineage, links, log), and today they are interleaved down one column. Hierarchy & Links absorbs Lineage, Hierarchy, Team initiatives and Links — which is what those sections already are; Activity absorbs the Log, including the note composer that moves to the sticky footer. The active tab is panel-local state, not persisted app state. DETAILS TAB. A two-column property grid of four labelled cells: Status, Priority, Initiative lead, Estimate and target. Status is DERIVED from the lane and the rollup, so it renders as a read-only chip and never as a select — the single most important adaptation in the reference, because if it looks like a dropdown it will be treated as one. Priority is the field from task 56, which this depends on. Initiative lead is `assignees`, plural here, so allow more than the reference single avatar. Estimate is the existing `size` and target is `targetStartDate`/`targetEndDate`; the reference pairs them in one cell, which suits two small values. Then a STRATEGIC IMPACT card: the objective the work serves, its key result, and progress. Hold the rule — OKRs attach to strategic initiatives only, so a card shows the mapping it INHERITS through the lineage and never gains a direct one; the card should say that rather than offering a link. The reference On Track label has no field behind it, so either derive a health signal from progress against the key result target and current, or drop the label and show the number alone — do not add a status field. Then PRODUCT SPECIFICATION: the description rendered as markdown with an Edit affordance, plus optional callout boxes (the reference uses Primary Hypothesis and Non-Goals). Those callouts are supporting notes rather than fields, so they need a real home — a second description field, or a convention inside the markdown — or they are decoration. Then SUB-TASKS: the decomposition children as rows (derived status dot, ref, title, status chip, avatars) with an inline add. Then ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA: the existing checklist with a done count and a progress bar. FOOTER. A sticky comment composer — a textarea with an attach affordance and Send, plus the reference hint line (Press M to leave a quick comment, Markdown supported). It writes through the existing note path into the item log, so a comment is a log entry rather than a new entity, and the Activity count grows with it. The reference shows an attachment affordance; there is no backend, so that becomes a link field or is dropped. Escape and the close button keep working; the drawer already leaves the board visible, so no new dismissal behaviour is needed. DELIVERED: the drawer keeps its place and is now 460px with a compact header (lineage breadcrumb, focus/more/close, type/ref/board chips, Mark Blocked, editable title) and three tabs — Details, Hierarchy & Links, Activity — each carrying a count. Details holds the two-column property grid, a strategic-impact card, the product specification with a Write/Preview toggle, sub-tasks as rows with derived status chips, and acceptance criteria with a progress bar. Mark Blocked expands to a reason field rather than dropping it. The more menu holds type, archive and delete. A sticky composer writes through the existing note path into the item log. Adaptations actually made: Status is a read-only chip; Priority became a real field (see task 56); the reference callouts (Primary Hypothesis / Non-Goals) were dropped rather than faked, since they need a field or a markdown convention; the copy-link and watch icons became focus and more; attachment was dropped (no backend). Verified over CDP on a card and an initiative, tab switching, and the composer writing a log entry.
tasks.testStrategy: Behavioural check over CDP using the existing `data-item-panel` hook: open a card and an initiative and confirm the header, tab strip and property grid render for both; switch tabs and confirm the section groups move with them; confirm Escape and the close button each clear `selectedItemId`. Assert Status is read-only and that no control in the panel writes a derived value. Confirm the comment composer writes a log entry and that the Activity count increments. Re-verify every surface that deep-links into the panel (`?item=`, dashboard rows, timeline bars) still opens it, and that the board behind is left in a clean state after close. Run npm test and npm run build.

tasks.title: Pan the board by dragging empty workflow space
tasks.description: P1: drag any empty part of a workflow to pan the board — for navigating flows wider than the screen, and to stop a drag on the board from becoming a text selection.
tasks.details: Both workflows scroll — BoardCanvas and BoardSummary sit inside an overflow container — but the only way to move sideways is the scrollbar, and a drag on empty board surface starts a text selection instead, which is the opposite of what it looks like it should do. Make a press on empty workflow space start a pan: the cursor becomes a grabbing hand, the container scrolls with the pointer, and text selection is suppressed for the duration. It must not disturb anything already draggable — cards, initiatives, lanes and the edit-mode controls — so a pan only begins when the press lands on the workflow surface itself and not on a card, a cell's interactive content, or a control. Clicks must keep working: a press that does not move is still a click (deselect, close the panel, clear focus), so the pan needs a small movement threshold before it engages. Touch and trackpad pan natively, so scope this to pointer devices and leave the scrollbar as it is. Worth doing for the cards workflow and the initiatives flow in one go — they share the scroll container shape — and for the boundary panel if it scrolls independently. DELIVERED: usePanScroll in src/lib, wired to the cards canvas, the board view and the coordination view. Pointer capture on press so a fast drag keeps panning; a four-pixel threshold so a motionless press is still a click; select-none while panning; grab/grabbing cursor. Verified with synthetic pointer events: empty-space drag scrolls and stays, motionless press still opens a card, a drag from a card moves neither.
tasks.testStrategy: Behavioural check over CDP: a drag on empty workflow space scrolls the container and leaves no text selected; a drag that starts on a card still moves the card and never pans; a press with no movement still behaves as a click; the edit-mode lane controls still work. Verify both workflows. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Legibility — a type scale and a contrast floor
tasks.description: Usability, and the one felt on every screen: much of the interface is set too small and too pale to read comfortably. The item panel is the worst of it, but the top bar and the card faces have the same problem. This is not a matter of taste — 10px text and slate-400 on white are below the thresholds at which text is reliably readable.
tasks.details: The offenders, counted: 37 uses of `text-[9px]`, 115 of `text-[10px]` and 129 of `text-[11px]`, and as text colour 141 uses of `slate-400` and 22 of `slate-300`. On white that is about 2.6:1 and 1.7:1 — under the 4.5:1 that normal text needs and under the 3:1 that even large text needs, so the palest labels are decoration rather than text. By file the weight sits where it is felt: ItemPanel 88 tiny-text uses, then Card 17, BoardCanvas 14, BoardWorkspace 11, TopBar 6. Two changes, and neither is a redesign. First a type scale in `@theme` — a handful of named steps replacing three hundred arbitrary `text-[Npx]` values, so a size is chosen rather than guessed and the floor can be raised once. Second a contrast floor: the lightest colour allowed for content is `slate-500` (about 4.8:1 on white), and `slate-400` and `slate-300` are reserved for what is not text — icons, dividers, disabled states. The floor itself: nothing below 11px, and 12px for anything read as a sentence. Raising the sizes reflows the card face, which is a fixed 180px wide and already sheds detail through `@container` variants as its column narrows, so those need re-checking — and the standing rule that a lane header wraps rather than truncates still holds. Contrast must be measured against what text actually sits on, which is not white: the stage-tinted column surfaces (`STAGE_SURFACE`) and the tinted card faces (`hexToRgba(type.color, 0.1)` over white). Out of scope: dark mode, a new palette, any layout change, and the keyboard and screen-reader work, which is task 37 and is about semantics rather than legibility. DELIVERED: a five-step scale in @theme (micro 11 / meta 12 / body 13 / title 15 / heading 18) with 387 arbitrary sizes migrated onto it and nothing below micro; text moved to slate-600 or darker at 190 sites, with slate-500 and lighter reserved for icons, dividers and disabled states. The floor is slate-600 rather than slate-500 because slate-500 is 3.9:1 on a tinted column and 4.3:1 on slate-100 — it only clears 4.5:1 on white, which is not what text sits on. Both guards shipped and were checked by breaking them: a source test that names the file and line when a text-[Npx] returns, and a contrast test over the stage surfaces and every type chip. The contrast test found a real bug: the type chips picked their text colour by a brightness threshold, giving white on sky-500 at 2.8:1 and on amber-500 at 2.2:1; readableOn is now chipColors, choosing by contrast ratio and darkening the ground only when neither extreme reaches the floor. 142 tests, was 139.
tasks.testStrategy: Make the floor enforceable rather than aspirational, or it erodes again within a month. Two automated guards, both pure and fast: a source test asserting no `text-[9px]` or `text-[10px]` remains anywhere in `src` — it fails loudly the moment someone adds one back — and a contrast test computing WCAG ratios from the hex values in `src/lib/colors.ts` for every pair that actually meets on screen: body text on each stage surface, meta text on the card-face tints, and the column headers, asserting at least 4.5:1 for body and 3:1 for the largest. Then the visual pass, which no test replaces: screenshots of the item panel, the top bar and a card face before and after at 100% zoom, plus one card at each `@container` breakpoint to confirm the reflow did not push anything out of a fixed-width card. Run npm test.

tasks.title: A completed card and initiative are stamped Done
tasks.description: A visual indicator on the board: a green check that stamps a card or an initiative as Done, so a finished thing reads as finished at a glance rather than having to be inferred from the column it sits in.
tasks.details: The derivation already knows, and it knows for both shapes at once: `rollupOf(id, graph).bucket === 'done'` is true for a leaf sitting in a Done column and for a parent whose every leaf is done — the same rule the initiatives workflow arranges its sections by, so the stamp can never disagree with the column it is in. That matters more than it sounds: a stamp that contradicted the board would be worse than no stamp, and the one thing this must not do is claim completion early, which is the rule `rollupOf` already refuses to break. Show it on both card faces — the narrow card in a lane and the wide summary card in the initiatives workflow — as a filled emerald circle with a white check, in the header beside the priority badge. One mark, and the card surface itself is left alone: a Done column is already tinted, and re-tinting every card in it would turn the most finished part of the board into the loudest. A large watermark was considered and rejected for the same reason — it would eat into the legibility the last task bought. Out of scope: changing what Done means, and any new stored field. DELIVERED: isComplete in the domain (rollupOf bucket === done), used by both card faces; a 16px emerald check in the card header, before the priority badge. Tested hardest on the negatives, including the 100%-but-not-done case that would make the stamp lie. Verified in the browser: only the card already in Done is stamped as seeded, moving one card stamps only that one, and the initiative gains its stamp only once all five leaves finish. 144 tests, was 143.
tasks.testStrategy: The risk is a false positive, not a false negative, so test the negatives hardest: a card in a Done column is stamped; a card in Backlog, Not Started or In Progress is not; an initiative whose leaves are all done is stamped; an initiative with one leaf still open is not, even when every other leaf is done and its percentage reads 100 — which is exactly the case `rollupOf` exists to get right. Then a browser check that the mark renders on both card shapes and on nothing else, and a screenshot of a board with a Done column and a mixed initiatives flow to confirm it reads as an affirmation rather than as another badge.

tasks.title: Set a card’s parent from its context menu, by pointing at an initiative
tasks.description: Connect a card to an initiative from the card itself. The context menu gains a “Set parent” option which puts the board into a pick mode; clicking an initiative there sets it as the card’s parent, and the card’s roll-up chip appears. Only a card connects to an initiative — an initiative is never the child of a card.
tasks.details: The item panel already has a Parent section with a select, so this is the same act done from the board — where the card and the initiative are both on screen and you can see what you are connecting to. A dropdown of every item by name is the fallback; pointing at the actual initiative is the thing a board can do that a list cannot. The mechanics are small: the menu gains an option, choosing it sets a mode in the store, and a click on an initiative in that mode calls the existing `setParent`. One parent, always — `setParent` replaces rather than appends, so picking a second initiative moves the card rather than giving it two, and the menu should offer to remove an existing parent as well as set one. The rule this rests on needs enforcing first, and it is what makes a loop impossible rather than merely unlikely: **an initiative is never the child of a card**. Connections run one way — a card rolls up to an initiative, and an initiative's parent is another initiative — so going down the tree the type can only fall from initiative to card, and nothing can ever be its own ancestor. That is a stronger and simpler answer than asking a picker to refuse a card's own subtree, and it belongs in the store, where every path already goes through it: `setParent` refuses an initiative whose parent is not an initiative. The panel's Parent select already excludes the item's own descendants — so it cannot make a loop either — but it offers every other item by name, including a card as an initiative's parent, so it is the half that is missing and should follow the same rule. The picker then needs no exclusion list at all — it offers initiatives, and a card cannot be a parent by construction. Only initiatives are offered, since a card rolls up to an outcome. The mode is the shape `boundaryId` already has — one id in the store, Escape to cancel, the board reads it — and a second mechanism for the same idea would be one too many. Feedback after picking: the card's roll-up chip, and the panel's Parent section if the card is open. Out of scope: changing what a parent means, setting parents for a whole selection at once, and the initiative side of the connection, which already has its own way in. DELIVERED: the rule lives in setParent, so every path gets it; the picker and the panel’s Parent select offer initiatives for the same reason. Pick mode dims everything that is not a choice and leaves the initiative lit; a click on a card does nothing and keeps the mode open. The initiative cards answer the pick from the initiatives workflow, which is where they are. Verified in the browser with real input. 150 tests, was 149.
tasks.testStrategy: The type rule first, because it is what makes the rest safe: an initiative whose parent would be a card is refused; an initiative under an initiative is allowed; a card under an initiative is allowed; a card under a card is allowed — the rule is about where initiatives may sit, not about how deep cards go. With that in place a cycle is unreachable, so the test asserts the rule rather than trying to enumerate loops: the store refuses the one edge that could start one. Then that setting a parent replaces rather than adds, and that removing one leaves the card a root. Then the interaction in the browser, with real input: the menu offers Set parent, choosing it puts the board in the mode, clicking an initiative sets the parent and the card's chip appears, clicking a card does nothing at all because a card cannot be a parent, and Escape leaves the parent exactly as it was. Run npm test.

tasks.title: A context menu for initiatives, and connecting a card from the initiative end
tasks.description: Initiative cards have no context menu at all. Give them one, and in it the same act task 64 added for cards but from the other end: pick a card and it becomes a child of this initiative — one edge, set from whichever end you happen to be looking at.
tasks.details: Task 64 let a card name the initiative it rolls up to, from the card. This is the same edge named from the initiative: you are looking at an outcome and you want to pull work under it, which is the moment the connection is actually in your head. Both ends set one decomposition edge, so both must go through `setParent` and neither may invent a second kind of link. The rule holds unchanged and is what makes it safe: a parent is always an initiative, so an initiative may only ever take children, never a parent that is a card. Initiative cards currently pass no `onContextMenu` at all, so the menu is new — reuse `CardMenu` rather than writing a second one, since most of what it offers (priority, assignees, size, dates, block, archive) applies to an initiative too, and the card-only entries are already guarded. The pick is the shape task 64 used: a mode in the store, a floating chip saying what to do, Escape to cancel, and the board resolving a click. The difference is which end is being chosen — there, an initiative among dimmed cards; here, a card among dimmed initiatives — so the mode needs a direction rather than a second mechanism, and the same `parentPickId` should grow one rather than being duplicated. Clicking anything that is not a valid choice does nothing and leaves the mode open, as before. Feedback after picking: the card appears as a child in the initiative's Hierarchy & Links, and its own roll-up chip appears on the card. DELIVERED: the wide card never wired onContextMenu, which is why initiatives had no menu at all; they have one now, reusing CardMenu. Connect a card… starts a mode that dims the initiatives and lights the cards — the same parentPick shape with a direction rather than a second mechanism. Verified in the browser with real input. 152 tests.
tasks.testStrategy: The rule first, unchanged and already tested: a parent is always an initiative, so connecting a card to an initiative is allowed and connecting an initiative to a card is not — assert the second is refused, because that is the one this feature makes easy to attempt from the wrong end. Then that both directions produce exactly one decomposition edge: connecting from the initiative and then from the card names the same edge, not two. Then the interaction in the browser with real input: an initiative has a context menu, the connect option puts the board in a pick mode, clicking a card sets the parent and closes the mode, clicking an initiative does nothing and keeps it open, and Escape leaves the graph exactly as it was. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Connect a team initiative to a management one, from a Program board
tasks.description: A Program board shows each linked board as a band, and a band is read-only today — not by policy but because the context menu has nowhere to render there. Allow the one act that belongs on this surface: a team initiative in a band rolling up to a management initiative on the board itself.
tasks.details: Measured rather than assumed: on a Program board a right-click opens nothing at all. The reason is structural — `CardMenu` is rendered by `BoardCanvas`, and an aggregating board does not render `BoardCanvas`, so the menu has nowhere to appear. The same is true of the floating chip the pick mode shows. So the first move is to hoist the menu and the chip out of the cards canvas into something both surfaces mount, rather than rendering a second menu for aggregation. The band already passes `boardId`, and the pick already sets a parent through `setParent`, which is board-agnostic — so the connection itself needs nothing new. What it needs is a narrower set of choices: the pick must offer only the initiatives *on the board being viewed*, or a band could parent another band and the act stops being the flight-level one. `initiativeCellOf(id, boardId, graph)` already answers that — it is undefined for an item that is not on that board — so the guard is a lookup rather than a new rule. Drag stays off the bands, deliberately: a drag is a move, and moving another board's initiative from here edits a board you are not looking at. Its section restriction would be the only guard, and a lens should not move things. Out of scope: making bands editable in general, and the reverse act of linking from the management end, which the item panel already offers. PARTLY DELIVERED: CardMenu and the pick chips moved into an Overlays host mounted by App, so an aggregating board has them — verified that a band initiative opens a menu offering Set parent and that the chip appears. The scoping rule is in too, with viewedBoardId so a band knows which board is being looked at rather than assuming its own. REMAINING, and unverified: clicking a management initiative completing the connection, and clicking another band initiative being refused. The probe closed the mode on a band click, which the guard should have prevented, and there was no room left to find the real click path. DELIVERED: CardMenu and the pick chips moved into an Overlays host mounted by App, so an aggregating board has them; the choices are the initiatives on the board being viewed, with viewedBoardId so a band knows which board that is. The guard originally used initiativeCellOf, which falls back to a section first cell and so answered yes for another board entirely — it checks the placement now. Verified on a Program board: band initiatives dim to 0.4 while the board own stay at 1, a band click leaves the graph unchanged and the mode open, and a management click sets the parent and closes it. 151 tests.
tasks.testStrategy: The scoping rule first, because it is the whole of the new behaviour: the pick offers the initiatives on the board being viewed and not the band's, so a team initiative can be connected to a management one and two band initiatives cannot be connected to each other. Then that the act produces one decomposition edge and that the rule still holds from this surface — a parent is always an initiative. Then the interaction in the browser with real input: on a Program board a band's initiative has a context menu, the option puts the board in a pick mode with the chip visible, clicking a management initiative sets the parent and closes the mode, clicking another band's initiative does nothing and leaves it open, and Escape leaves the graph unchanged. Run npm test.

tasks.title: Bug: a card's drop shadow outlives the drop and takes up space on the board
tasks.description: After dropping a card, the insertion-gap placeholder stays in the lane — above the dropped card, occupying a slot — until the next drag begins.
tasks.details: Reported with a screenshot: after dropping Build signup form into a DONE column, the shadow placeholder sits above it and the card reads as moved below the shadow. ROOT CAUSE: BoardCanvas holds the gap in its own state (dropAt, set by onMove) and nothing ever clears it — onDrop resolves the gap and moves the card but never setDropAt(null), and there is no cleanup when the lift ends. The lane then renders at={ctx.drag.laneId === lane.id ? ctx.drag.index : null} with no guard on a lift being live, so once the gesture is over (lift null, draggingId null, the dropped card back in the list) the placeholder still renders at that index in that lane — above the card that now occupies the slot. It looks intermittent but it is every drop: it heals only when the next drag's first onMove overwrites dropAt. FIX SHAPE: gate the drag preview on the gesture being live — the lifting flag (lift !== null) already exists in BoardCanvas, so ctx.drag's laneId/index should read null when it is not — and clear dropAt in onDrop for hygiene. BoardSummary's dropCell has the same never-cleared shape and needs the same gate, otherwise fixing cards leaves the same latent bug in the initiatives workflow.
tasks.testStrategy: Browser probe with real input (Input.dispatchMouseEvent — synthetic DragEvents bypass the machinery): press a card, move it over a lane gap, release, then assert no [data-drop-placeholder] remains anywhere in the document, and that the landed lane's children are exactly its cards with no extra block. Repeat for a cross-lane move and a drop back into the origin lane.

tasks.title: Bug: initiative drags never show a drop target, where cards show the gap they would land in
tasks.description: Dragging an initiative gives no live drop feedback at all — no placeholder in the target cell — while a dragged card shows the insertion gap following the pointer.
tasks.details: Reported alongside the stale-card-shadow bug. ROOT CAUSE: a stale closure, not a missing render. BoardSummary's drag callback reads the dragged item as lift?.itemId — but useCardLift registers its pointermove listener once, at pointerdown, with the closure from that render, and never re-registers; lift only becomes non-null DURING the first move. So lift?.itemId is null for the entire drag, cellUnder cannot resolve the dragged initiative's own cell (here = undefined) and bails, dropCell never sets, and the placeholder in Cell never renders. The drop itself still lands correctly because onDrop receives itemId as a parameter rather than reading lift — which is exactly why this survived: the one path that works hides the one that does not. Cards were immune by accident: BoardCanvas's gapUnder reads the DOM (elementFromPoint, data-card-id), no React state, so its onMove closure going stale costs it nothing. FIX SHAPE: useCardLift already knows the itemId — pass it to onMove(itemId, x, y) so no callback ever reads lift through a stale closure; BoardCanvas's onMove ignores the extra argument. DESIGN CONSTRAINT when fixing: initiative cells have no order — a per-position gap inside a cell would be meaningless, so the intended feedback is the cell-level shadow (the placeholder at the top of the target cell, which already exists in Cell behind isTarget), not a card-style insertion gap. Dragging within an initiative's own cell deliberately shows nothing (there is no within-cell reorder to preview); decide whether that silence is right or whether the origin cell should say 'stays here'.
tasks.testStrategy: Browser probe with real input: press an initiative, move it over another cell of its own section, and assert the target cell renders [data-drop-placeholder] BEFORE release (during pointermove); assert it is gone after release. Also assert a move over a different section's cell and over the origin cell show nothing, and that the drop still moves the initiative.
